name: Common face rule
statement: \text{If a face appears in the same position in two views, the faces in matching positions are opposite each other.}
conditions: The common face must be in the same position (top, left or right) in both views.
derivation: Each view shows three faces meeting at a corner, in a fixed clockwise order.
Turn view 2 about the axis through the common face until it sits like view 1; the common face stays in place.
If the common face is already in the same position, the views differ only by that turn, so the face in each other position is replaced by its partner.
A face that leaves a position goes round the side ring; the face that took its place is not adjacent to it in either view, so they are opposite.
visual_proof: Two dice drawn side by side with the shared face in the same slot; arrows link the top faces and the other side faces as opposite pairs.
shortcut: Same face, same position → the other two pairs of positions give opposite faces directly.

steps: View 1: top Q, left Z, right V. View 2: top T, left L, right V.
V is common and on the right in both.
Top ↔ top: Q opposite T; left ↔ left: Z opposite L (so V opposite A).

common_traps: Using the rule when the common face is in different positions: gives wrong pairs (use [[f:dice.cyclic-order]] then).
Pairing top with left: gives Q opposite L, not an option, or Z.
Picking the common face itself (V) as the opposite.

diagram.alt_text: Table of the two dice views with V on the right in both; tops Q and T are opposite, lefts Z and L are opposite.

name: Adjacent-face elimination
statement: \text{Every face shown together with face } X \text{ is adjacent to it; the one face never seen with } X \text{ is opposite } X.
derivation: A cube face has 4 adjacent faces and 1 opposite face.
Two faces visible in the same view share an edge, so they are adjacent.
Once 4 different faces are seen with X, the sixth face is its opposite.
Remove that pair and repeat: a face already paired cannot be anyone else's opposite.
visual_proof: A table lists each face with the faces seen beside it; a row with four neighbours leaves exactly one face out, its opposite.
shortcut: Start with the face that appears in the most views; it usually has 4 neighbours shown.

steps: 25 is seen with 21, 23, 22, 24, so 25 is opposite 26.
21 is seen with 23, 25, 22; its opposite is 24 or 26, and 26 is taken.

common_traps: Answering 26 because it never appears: it is opposite 25, not 24 (A).
Treating faces in different views as adjacent just because they share a slot.
Stopping when a face has only 3 neighbours shown: two candidates remain until another pair is fixed.

diagram.alt_text: Table of faces 21 to 26, the faces seen next to each, and the opposite face that is left.

name: Cyclic order of faces
statement: \text{Read the visible faces of each view in clockwise order, line the views up on a shared face, and fill the ring round it.}
derivation: The four faces adjacent to a face X form a ring round it; opposite faces sit two apart in that ring.
Each view shows X with two neighbours that are next to each other in the ring, in a fixed direction.
Write each view's pair in the same direction (e.g. left then right) as a step of the ring.
Join the steps into one ring of four; faces two apart are opposite, and the face never seen with X is opposite X.
visual_proof: A ring of four faces drawn round the common top face: each view adds one arrow (left → right), and the arrows close into S → M → P → R.
shortcut: With the common face in the same slot, ring order is view 1 (left, right) then view 2 (left, right); 1st and 3rd are opposite, 2nd and 4th are opposite.

steps: T is on top in both views, so S, M, P, R surround T and C is opposite T.
Clockwise steps: S → M and P → R, so the ring is S, M, P, R.

common_traps: Answering C because it is never seen: C is opposite T, the common face (A).
Reading one view left → right and the other right → left: gives M opposite P (D).
Pairing faces in the same position (S with P) and stopping there without checking which pair includes M.

diagram.alt_text: Table of the ring round T: views give S then M and P then R; opposite pairs S-P, M-R, T-C.

name: Cube net opposite faces
statement: \text{In a net, two squares in one straight row or column with exactly one square between them are opposite; touching squares are never opposite.}
conditions: The net must fold into a cube (6 squares, no overlap).
derivation: Folding along the edge between two touching squares makes them meet at that edge, so they are adjacent.
In a straight line of three squares, the middle one becomes a side and the outer two fold up on either side of it.
Those two outer squares end up parallel, facing each other: opposite.
For a square sticking out of a column, slide it along the fold to the end square it would cover, then use the same rule.
visual_proof: A column of four with one square on each side: # and €, % and ∞ are one apart in the column, and the two side squares @ and * fold to face each other.
shortcut: Alternate squares in a straight line are opposite; the two squares left after that are each other's opposite.

steps: # and € have one square between them in the column: opposite.

common_traps: Taking a touching square as opposite: @ (A) or % (D) share an edge with #.
Taking the far end of a column of four (∞): squares two apart in a line are adjacent (B).
Applying the rule along a bent path instead of a straight line.

diagram.alt_text: Cube net: a column #, %, €, ∞ with @ to the left of # and * to the right of ∞; opposite pairs #-€, %-∞, @-*.

name: Painted cube counting
statement: n\times n\times n \text{ painted cube cut into } n^3 \text{ unit cubes: 3 faces} = 8,\ \text{2 faces} = 12(n-2),\ \text{1 face} = 6(n-2)^2,\ \text{0 faces} = (n-2)^3
derivation: A unit cube has one painted face for each of its coordinates that lies on an outer layer (first or last of $n$).
Along one axis there are 2 outer layers and $n-2$ inner ones.
3 painted faces: all three coordinates outer, $2^3 = 8$ corners.
2 painted faces: choose the inner axis (3 ways), $3 \cdot 2^2 (n-2) = 12(n-2)$, the edge cubes.
1 painted face: $3 \cdot 2 (n-2)^2 = 6(n-2)^2$; none: $(n-2)^3$, the hidden inner cube.
visual_proof: A cube with its 8 corners, 12 edges (n - 2 cubes each) and 6 faces ((n - 2)^2 each) marked; the inner (n - 2)^3 block stays unpainted.
shortcut: Corners 8, edges $12(n-2)$, faces $6(n-2)^2$, core $(n-2)^3$: one number per part of the cube.
common_traps: Using $n$ instead of $n-2$ on each edge: counts the corners twice, e.g. 48 instead of 24 two-face cubes for $n = 4$.
Using $(n-1)^3$ for the unpainted core: for $n = 4$ gives 27 instead of 8.
Applying the formula at $n = 1$: the single cube has 6 painted faces, not 8 corners.

diagram.alt_text: A cube of side n split into unit cubes, with labels for corners (3 faces), edges (2 faces), face centres (1 face) and the hidden core (0 faces).
